items.title: AI agents are starting to fill out medical forms and file insurance requests in place of human staff
items.desc: OpenAI wants GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Luna to automate administrative tasks in US healthcare through computer-use agents that operate existing clinic software and insurance portals the way a human would. Luna handles tasks like prior authorizations for about 8.5 cents each. Companies including CVS Health and Cigna Healthcare are already deploying the technology. The article AI agents are starting to fill out medical forms and file insurance requests in place of human staff appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI wants GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Luna to click and type their way through clinic software and insurance portals as digital clerks. GPT-6 Luna handles administrative tasks for about 8.5 cents per task, according to the company. In a recent product announcement , OpenAI targets the lack of APIs in healthcare. The computer-use agents integrated into the Agents API in late September operate existing user interfaces the way a human would. In this case, they transfer data between electronic health records and external web portals. According to OpenAI, when a patient reports back pain, the agent is meant to search relevant prior findings and draft both an MRI order and a reply to the patient. It should also prepare a prior authorization request on the insurer's portal. Clinicians and the responsible administrative staff review these drafts before they are released. The features are available through the API as well as in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians. Ad In an evaluation described by OpenAI, GPT-6 Astra worked through tasks from electronic health record inboxes, among other things preparing an ibuprofen dosage for a child with a broken arm. Physician reviewers rated 99 percent of the 325 tasks evaluated as clinically safe. In 93 percent of 646 reviews, the reviewers called the prep work very or extremely helpful. For administrative workflows such as prior authorizations, appeals, or medical equipment orders, OpenAI points to the independent HealthAdminBench benchmark from Stanford University researchers . GPT-6 Astra scored 94.3 percent of possible points. GPT-6 Luna, built for low API pricing , scored 91.8 percent and, according to OpenAI, cost about 8.5 cents per task, 98 percent less than Astra. Both models ran at maximum reasoning effort on the benchmark. Ad Several partner organizations are helping advance the technology. At CVS Health, the agents already process referrals and specialist consultations across separate systems. According to the announcement, one agent cleared a months-long backlog of outgoing documents in one weekend, while another handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consultations daily. CVS Health published its software architecture as Agent Kit on GitHub. At insurer Cigna Healthcare, the models merge patient information from more than 10 separate systems. Abridge is developing the agents for planned use in clinical discharge planning. Ambience has demonstrated additional safety mechanisms in which an agent stops when a patient's record is unclear and asks a physician for input. Startups like Assort also use the feature in Codex to complete referrals in practice management software whose APIs don't support that final click. Ad Because the agents work directly in electronic health records, protecting sensitive health data is a core concern. OpenAI says it does not use organizational data to train its base models. ChatGPT for Healthcare offers role-based access controls and audit logs, according to the company. Organizations can also configure the applications and environments so an agent only accesses the records and actions needed for a given task. Ad For HIPAA-compliant workflows with protect

items.full: OpenAI is giving NATO and several European governments access to its cybersecurity tool Daybreak. Through Daybreak , cyber defense teams can use OpenAI's models to audit software, find vulnerabilities, and patch security gaps. The NATO Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) says it's already using the underlying models heavily. NCIA chief Dylan Browne called it a generational leap in cyber defense. During the NATO exercise Crossed Swords 2026 , participants deployed AI agents for cyber operations under human oversight for the first time. The models have already delivered results elsewhere. The EU's cybersecurity agency ENISA used them to find four vulnerabilities in software used by EU institutions. A joint report with CERT-EU examined 27 software projects, and 95 percent of the 88 reported issues turned out to be real bugs. Poland's CERT Polska found six vulnerabilities in MikroTik routers that were being actively exploited. Ukraine is using Daybreak to protect civilian infrastructure. France, Germany, and Poland have also been granted access. items.title: Reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material have surged more than 8,400 percent in two years
items.desc: Edinburgh's Childlight Institute reports a more than 8,400 percent increase in AI-generated child sexual abuse material over two years, from about 4,700 reports in 2023 to over 400,000 in 2025. Abusers are using tools like nudify apps for blackmail. Childlight CEO Paul Stanfield wants governments to classify the problem as a preventable public health emergency. The article Reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material have surged more than 8,400 percent in two years appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Reports of AI being used for the sexual exploitation of children have jumped more than 8,400 percent in two years. According to a report by Edinburgh's Childlight Institute, the number of reported AI-generated abuse images climbed from about 4,700 in 2023 to over 400,000 in 2025, The Guardian reports . The material includes AI-manipulated images (deepfakes) from so-called "nudify apps" that digitally strip people of their clothing. Abusers can use the faked images to blackmail children into handing over money or more photos. The data comes from reports that tech companies filed with the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC). The UK's Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) reviewed 6,310 criminal, photorealistic AI-generated abuse images in the first half of 2026 alone. That's 40 percent more than in all of 2025. Childlight data director Debi Fry acknowledges that better detection systems partly explain the spike. She still calls for swift action from lawmakers and tech companies. Childlight CEO Paul Stanfield wants governments to classify the problem as a preventable public health emergency, dedicate funding to prevention, and coordinate efforts across healthcare, schools, child protection services, and the justice system. items.title: Why operational visibility is becoming more valuable than performance scores
items.desc: Your client’s WooCommerce homepage scores 98 in Lighthouse. They’re happy with that, until a customer emails: “I enter my delivery address, and checkout just sits there.” ...
items.full: Your client’s WooCommerce homepage scores 98 in Lighthouse. They’re happy with that, until a customer emails: “I enter my delivery address, and checkout just sits there.” You try it yourself. Everything works. By the following afternoon, another complaint arrives. The homepage still loads quickly, and another speed test gives you little to investigate. Somewhere in the live site, under conditions your test doesn’t reproduce, customers struggle to place an order. Performance reports are more than just a simple score, though. Your team needs to know what runs during the slowdown and where requests spend their time. Otherwise, troubleshooting becomes a sequence of guesses, each with its own chance of disrupting the store. As sites take on more automated work, those questions become harder to answer from the browser alone. This article follows that checkout problem from the first complaint through the fix, with a look at the evidence your agency needs and how to explain the results to a client. A Lighthouse report earns its place in a developer’s toolkit. It can expose a large image that delays the main content or JavaScript that keeps the browser busy. Fixing those problems improves the experience people have on the page. The performance score combines several measurements from the test. It’s useful for comparing changes under similar conditions, provided you pay attention to the individual metrics behind it. The trouble starts when a client reads “98” as confirmation that everything on the website works well. A standard homepage audit doesn’t usually involve filling a cart and submitting a shipping address. It doesn’t wait for the afternoon inventory update, either. Instead, it measures the page you ask it to test, under the conditions of that run. PageSpeed Insights also includes field data from the Chrome User Experience Report when enough data is available. That reflects real visitors over a rolling 28-day period. The Lighthouse score comes from a separate lab test. Mixing those up makes the report harder to explain. Real-user Core Web Vitals give you a broader view of page experience. They still don’t identify which function inside an import plugin puts pressure on the database. For the store in our example, the homepage score can be entirely legitimate. A cached page reaches visitors quickly while checkout waits on work inside WordPress. The useful question is whether your measurements cover the interaction customers complain about. A fast homepage tells you something worth knowing. It leaves plenty of the store untested. At 2 p.m., the store imports a supplier’s stock file. Nobody opens the WordPress dashboard to start it. A scheduled task begins processing product records while customers continue shopping. That import needs database time. Depending on how the plugin runs it, it also occupies PHP threads that serve other requests. Moving work into the background changes when it happens, but the work still uses resources. WordPress cron jobs and queue runners can make this activity easy to overlook. The schedule lives in a plugin setting, and the person who configures it may have no reason to revisit it until something slows down. AI agent

items.title: AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?
items.desc: AI has sped up how teams design and build, but quality assurance (QA) testing hasn’t kept pace, and the web may be getting less accessible. Drawing on new research, Andrew Chung explains what separates the teams whose accessibility efforts are keeping up, and how to embed human judgment into AI-enabled workflows without slowing delivery.
items.full: About The Author Andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access , a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms. Andrew leads the … More about Andrew ↬ Weekly tips on front-end & UX . Trusted by 182,000+ folks. This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access , who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you! Lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report . Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up. We asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most said they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage. These results point to a two-speed workflow . AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible? Accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now. This matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor. So how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace? We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently. Here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge shows up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training , communication , and a culture of accessibility . A quick caveat : This is survey data, so it only shows correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore. And it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize issues. items.title: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra tackles the Standard Model's toughest math problem on a lattice
items.desc: OpenAI physicist Nathaniel Craig used GPT-6 Astra to tackle a problem that had stumped particle physicists for over 25 years. The AI model took Craig's strategy for defining the full Standard Model on a computational lattice and turned it into a working proof. Craig says a lot of work remains before realistic simulations are possible. The article OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra tackles the Standard Model's toughest math problem on a lattice appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra helped produce a proof that could solve a 50-year-old problem in particle physics. Physicist Nathaniel Craig of UC Santa Barbara, currently a visiting scientist at OpenAI, presented the approach on the OpenAI blog and as a preprint paper . Craig leads the particle theory group at UCSB and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics. Physicists can simulate parts of the Standard Model, the theory describing all known particles and fundamental forces, on a computer grid called a lattice. That has already led to breakthroughs like calculating the proton's mass from first principles. But putting the full theory on a lattice has been impossible. The weak force, which governs certain types of radioactive decay, treats left- and right-handed particles differently. On simple lattices, this asymmetry creates unwanted ghost particles. Special lattice particles called overlap fermions can filter them out, but for over 25 years, nobody could set their phase correctly. Ad Craig had a strategy to fix the phase by comparing progressively finer lattices, but couldn't prove it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. GPT-6 Astra turned the idea into a working construction and took the lead on the detailed proof. Lattice field theorists Maarten Golterman, Andreas Kronfeld, and Yigal Shamir reviewed the proof and raised questions that Craig says helped build confidence in the result. He calls the work "much more a beginning than an end" and says a lot remains before realistic simulations are possible. Ad The result follows a run of AI advances in mathematics that started in January 2026 . In May, OpenAI's disproof of Erdős's unit distance conjecture became the first AI proof worthy of math's top journal . Days later, Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Nexus solved nine of 353 open Erdős problems for a few hundred dollars, and by October its results had passed peer review . The most far-reaching claim came in September, when OpenAI submitted a 166-page proof for the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem and the Clay Mathematics Institute said it had "apparently been settled" . The solution remains under review, and mathematicians have questioned whether OpenAI fully understands its own proof . Across the field, mathematicians have mixed feelings as AI keeps cracking unsolved problems. items.title: Staggering Scroll-Driven Animations with animation-range-start
items.desc: Imagine a CSS karaoke machine that displays a ball bouncing on text that incrementally highlights, based on progress through via speech recognition and running that kind of animation as a single predictable, holistic effect driven by one progress value. Staggering Scroll-Driven Animations with animation-range-start originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. The other day on the CSS-Tricks Slack channel, Danny Schwartz shared an interesting recent Master.dev article by Ashutosh Biswas on how to stagger CSS scrolling animations using a clever combo of several emergent CSS features and a lot of math, which Ashutosh admits is “a huge formula and can look intimidating.” I’ll agree with Ashutosh there. A heartbreaking work of staggering genius When Danny Slacked the link for the Frontend Masters article, he described it as “CSS on drugs.” Speaking of drugs, I am on heavy prescription painkillers while recovering from a serious injury, so that might not help my current comprehension skills. Nevertheless, after reading Ashutosh’s article a few times, here’s a meme showing how I’d feel using such an elaborate algorithm for something as mundane as staggering the animations of some characters as they scroll into view. Don’t get me wrong. I know the complexity is because Ashutosh is going for a generic solution in which we can connect a “progress value to an animation, scroll progress, or any other input to drive the staggering.” In fact, I can dream up a scenario in which this might be what we want: Imagine a CSS karaoke machine that displays a ball bouncing on text that incrementally highlights, based on the user’s progress through the vocals measured via speech recognition . Running that kind of animation “not as a collection of independently timed objects, but as a single predictable, holistic effect driven by one progress value” might be exactly what the doctor ordered. This would be true because the staggered animations could be interrelated, and the overall animation would be driven by a custom input that’s not built into the browser. But unlike this hypothetical scenario, replacing the passage of time with scroll progress to control animations is already built into modern CSS. I contend that we’d need a better reason to roll our own implementation than the examples Ashutosh gives. How modern CSS solves staggered scrolling animations Ashutosh showcases a scroll-driven use case as “one of those ideal scenarios where the stagger formula shines.” But a red flag that we’re in danger of reinventing something we can get for free is that the spec for scroll-driven animations is cognizant that if we opt to base an animation on scroll progress rather than on time, then, as Ashutosh says, “the animation we are going to achieve is different from traditional ones because we don’t include time in our considerations.” This is no surprise to the creators of scroll timeline, and the MDN docs make Ashutosh’s point in different words when introducing scroll timeline . The docs also point out that animation-delay is only meaningful when we are using the default time-based document timeline . Therefore, animation-delay does not affect scroll-driven animations. But this is why CSS introduced animation-range-start , which allows us to delay a scroll-driven animation relative to scroll progress and not time. items.title: Anthropic says the key to agent memory is knowing what to forget, not how much to store
items.desc: Anthropic studied how Claude retains knowledge across sessions. Selective notes beat exhaustive archives by a wide margin. In a Pokémon Red test, the newer Claude Fable 5 got four times as far as the older Sonnet 3.7 by keeping just a handful of strategy files instead of more than 400. A "Dreaming" process retroactively corrects faulty memories. The article Anthropic says the key to agent memory is knowing what to forget, not how much to store appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Anthropic studied how Claude retains knowledge across sessions. Its tests show that selective notes outperform exhaustive archives and that having Claude review its own memories after the fact can correct errors. Anyone who works with an AI agent on a project over several days hits a wall fast, because every new session starts from scratch. In a research post, Anthropic describes how Claude is supposed to retain knowledge across sessions while the model stays unchanged. Claude writes notes to a folder that it can read back later. The core problem, according to Anthropic , is selection. Before it knows what comes next, the agent has to decide in the moment what might matter later, so every note is a bet on the future. Ad In an Anthropic test with Pokémon Red, the older Claude Sonnet 3.7 treated everything as potentially important and, across roughly 10,000 game steps, created 413 files in 225 folders, often a separate one for each battle and item it found. Because the game state keeps changing, the archive goes stale fast. At times, the model did nothing but reorganize its notes instead of playing, and it finished with just a single badge. Ad The newer Claude Fable 5 limited its memory to a few files and earned four badges. Fable 5 didn't record information already visible on screen and instead wrote down plans, strategies, and rules it had tested. Anthropic's comparison, however, covers only a single playthrough per model. Anthropic recommends explaining the purpose of memory to Claude and letting the model decide how to use it. In one benchmark, according to Anthropic, rigid instructions such as "only record mistakes" wiped out most of the advantage for stronger models. Older models, by contrast, benefited from clear instructions, such as being told to actually read their notes before every response. Ad The bigger risk comes from faulty notes that the agent blindly trusts later. Dreaming , an idea that builds on research from Letta and UC Berkeley, is designed to address this. Much like the human brain processes experiences during sleep, Claude goes through transcripts of earlier sessions during a break and checks its notes against them. In the Pokémon test, Claude had incorrectly noted which side of a mountain a landmark was on. Relying on that faulty note, Claude fell into the same trap three times, eventually wanted to give up, and missed its goal. After a Dreaming pass, Claude caught the error by checking the note against the transcript and found the right path. Ad According to Anthropic, Dreaming can also organize larger knowledge bases. Claude built a linked wiki from about 350,000 internal documents from Stainless, a software company Anthropic acquired. Dreaming is supposed to generate new pages while fixing gaps, duplicates, and broken links. The payoff was greatest when Claude could combine the wiki with search, so the wiki worked as a complement rather than a replacement. Ad In a separate legal test by Anthropic, a wiki helped most with questions whose answers were spread across multiple documents. items.full: I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-view-transition . content > . facet-results { view-transition-name : facet-results ; } /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */ html : active-view-transition . table-wrapper : has ( > table . rows-and-columns ) { view-transition-name : rows-table ; } With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.) items.title: The US wants to block China from renting AI power abroad but China already built a parallel supply chain from US AI output
items.desc: The US is tightening its chip export controls. Data centers in third countries like Singapore and Malaysia will soon need a US license to buy Nvidia chips, closing the loophole that let Chinese firms rent cloud compute abroad. A Reuters investigation also reveals how China offsets its hardware shortage through industrial-scale distillation of US AI models. The article The US wants to block China from renting AI power abroad but China already built a parallel supply chain from US AI output appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The US wants to block China from renting AI power abroad but China already built a parallel supply chain from US AI output Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner Nov 17, 2026 Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER Chinese companies have been skirting US export bans by legally renting Nvidia computing power in third countries. After Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, the US is closing that loophole. An investigation also reveals how China has cushioned the years-long chip embargo through an entire industry built around model distillation. For years, the US has tried to cut China off from importing advanced AI processors through strict export controls. Chinese companies responded by exploiting an entirely legal loophole, renting the computing power they needed through cloud-based remote access from foreign data centers that were allowed to receive US hardware. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) at the US Commerce Department now wants to shut down that workaround with an interim rule . It aligns remote-access rules with existing physical export bans. Data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil will need a US government license to buy advanced AI chips from US manufacturers like Nvidia, Bloomberg reports . Applications will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Subsidiaries of US-headquartered companies are exempt from the license requirement, as are shipments to data centers running only commercial recommendation systems for online retailers or social media platforms. The rules take effect once published in the Federal Register. Nvidia's stock fell as much as 2.9 percent after the announcement, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped up to 5.5 percent. The political trigger, though, was suspected illegal smuggling of physical chips. The new rule comes just days after the abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who had admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former manager at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. US authorities suspect Alice Huang, who now lives in China, of espionage. They are investigating Megaspeed for possible export-control violations after banned Nvidia chips reportedly turned up in a Chinese data center linked to her. Megaspeed denies any wrongdoing, and President Donald Trump said Monday that Jensen Huang did not compromise national security. The scandal still set off an open power struggle in Washington over lax enforcement of chip sanctions. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had delayed a Trump-authorized measure against illegal chip diversions, according to Axios, prompting Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to publicly accuse him of inaction. The Commerce Department's announcement now states with unusual bluntness that the draft rule was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council. A separate exclusive Reuters investigation shows how Chinese developers cope with the years-long shortage of top-tier domestic hardware.
